title: Preparing for a Hospice Care Plan Conversation
seoTitle: How to Prepare for a Hospice Care Plan Conversation
description: A simple way for families to prepare for a hospice care plan conversation: gather questions, describe changes at home and agree on the next steps together.
lede: A care plan conversation is a chance to tell the hospice team what daily life is like right now. You do not need a perfect list or medical language. A few notes about what has changed, what brings comfort and what feels difficult can help the team plan care around the person in front of them.

sections.heading: Start with what matters to the person receiving care
paragraphs: Ask what a good day feels like to them. Perhaps it means less pain, time with a loved one, a familiar routine or the chance to rest without interruption. Bring those wishes into the conversation, even if the person can only share them in a few words. If they cannot speak for themselves, tell the team what they have said in the past and who helps make decisions now.

A hospice care plan is personal and can change as needs change. The team can explain how nursing, social work, spiritual care and other support fit the goals you describe. Ask which parts of the plan can be adjusted if a routine is no longer working.

sections.heading: Bring observations instead of trying to diagnose
paragraphs: Write down changes you have noticed in comfort, sleep, breathing, eating, movement or mood. Include when a change began and what seems to help. Keep a current medication list nearby, including medicines from other clinicians. Tell the team about any equipment that is difficult to use and any caregiving task that feels unsafe.

You do not need to decide what a symptom means before calling. Describe what you see and let the nurse guide the clinical assessment. If something changes suddenly or causes concern, use the hospice team's on-call number rather than waiting for the next planned conversation.

sections.heading: Leave with a clear next step
paragraphs: Before the conversation ends, ask who to call for a new concern, what the team will do next and when you should expect to hear from them. It is reasonable to repeat the plan in your own words: “If this happens tonight, I call this number.” Ask for written instructions if they would help family members share responsibilities.

If a family member could not attend, decide together what information to pass along. A short shared note about the person's priorities and the team's next steps is often more helpful than trying to remember every detail. You can return to the conversation whenever goals or needs change.

ctaHeading: You can bring your questions to us
ctaCopy: Our team can listen to what is happening at home, explain how a care plan is made and help your family identify the next step.
